title: System Cleanup and Disk Usage
intro: Docker happily accumulates stopped containers, dangling images, and unused volumes forever unless you clean up — a dev machine that's been building images for months can easily have tens of gigabytes of dead weight.

steps.prompt: Check how much disk space Docker is actually using, broken down by category.
steps.fake_output:
TYPE            TOTAL   ACTIVE   SIZE      RECLAIMABLE
Images          42      3        18.2GB    15.1GB (82%)
Containers      12      2        450MB     380MB (84%)
Volumes         8       1        3.4GB     2.9GB (85%)
steps.explanation: 82% of image storage is reclaimable — that's old, unused image layers just sitting there.
steps.why: This is the equivalent of 'df -h' but scoped specifically to Docker's own storage — regular 'df -h' would show you the disk is full, but not that Docker specifically is the cause or what inside Docker is reclaimable.

steps.prompt: Remove all stopped containers, unused networks, and dangling images in one command.
steps.fake_output:
Deleted Containers: 10
Deleted Networks: 2
Total reclaimed space: 4.1GB
steps.explanation: This is the safe default cleanup — it does NOT touch volumes or images that are still tagged/referenced, only genuinely orphaned stuff.
steps.why: Notice this reclaimed only 4.1GB out of the 15.1GB the earlier system df showed as reclaimable for images alone — plain prune deliberately leaves tagged images alone, since those might still be intentionally kept around for a rollback.

steps.prompt: That wasn't enough. Remove ALL unused images too, not just dangling ones.
steps.explanation: -a is the more aggressive option — it removes any image not currently used by a running container, tagged or not.
steps.why: This is the one to think twice about on a shared machine — it'll delete images other people (or your own future self) might have been about to reuse, forcing a re-pull/re-build next time they're needed.

steps.prompt: Now clean up unused volumes specifically, since prune alone doesn't touch those.
steps.explanation: Volumes are the one category 'docker system prune' (without --volumes) deliberately skips, since they're the most likely thing to contain data you actually meant to keep.
steps.why: You could add --volumes to the original 'system prune' command instead of running this separately — it's broken out as its own command specifically because volume data loss is the one cleanup mistake that's hardest to undo, so it deserves a deliberate, separate step.
